extracted.intended_audience: general public; readers interested in literary ethics, journalism, and history
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing attribution, note-taking, and professional responses when plagiarism allegations arise in historical/biographical books. Focuses on what counts as improper borrowing and appropriate remediation and documentation practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper attribution/citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must give proper credit to sources; regularly cited sources nevertheless can contain sentence fragments that should have been in quotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As Goodwin admitted, 'While she was regularly cited, there were some sentence fragments that should have been in quotes.' Even when sources are cited, verbatim or near-verbatim language must be quoted or otherwise clearly indicated as sourced; failure to do so can lead to allegations and legal action (the article notes Goodwin and her publisher settled with plaintiff Lynne McTaggart).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish direct quotes from paraphrase
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers must be able to tell apart material that is a direct quotation from material that is paraphrased or original analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goodwin blamed mixing direct quotes and paraphrase in longhand notes, saying she 'couldn't tell them apart,' which resulted in whole sentences appearing in her book. The guidance is to ensure clear demarcation during note-taking (use quotation marks, clear labeling) so quoted language is not accidentally incorporated as the author’s own prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain provenance and organized notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep source material separately and maintain clear provenance for quoted text vs. analysis/notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goodwin says she now scans source text directly and keeps those files separate from her own notes and analysis. Best practice: segregate copies of source passages, use digital files or indexed notes that preserve original wording, and track which sentences are verbatim to avoid inadvertent borrowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document and publicly address allegations appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: When accused of improper borrowing, provide a transparent response that acknowledges specifics and corrective steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the St. Catherine's address Goodwin spoke only briefly to the controversy, admitting partial responsibility for borrowing. The implied standard is to clearly acknowledge the nature and extent of the problem and explain remedial measures (e.g., corrections, changes to research practice). Note that refusal to allow recording (Goodwin would not allow taping) may affect public perception of transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher and author responsibility to resolve claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers and authors should address claims of improper use of others' material, including legal settlements or corrections when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes a decade-old out-of-court settlement between Goodwin, her publisher Simon & Schuster, and Lynne McTaggart for using McTaggart's material without proper credit. This indicates a standard that such matters may require legal or formal resolution and that publishers share responsibility for addressing attribution failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly and journalistic scrutiny of excuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanations for improper borrowing are scrutinized by peers and journalists and may be judged inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gary Schwitzer, an assistant professor of journalism, attended the speech and said Goodwin's excuse is 'no excuse at all.' The criterion: defenses (e.g., poor note-taking) must be credible and accompanied by concrete corrective steps, otherwise they will be rejected by professional peers and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale of borrowing and proportional admission
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the extent of borrowed material (e.g., number of instances relative to manuscript length) and expect admissions or denials to address scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goodwin characterized the issue as 'out of a 1000 page manuscript, she drew in some small part from McTaggart.' Evaluators should consider both absolute and relative scale of borrowing when judging severity and appropriate remedies.
